coverage.assessment: Several premises are thinned. Paragraph 9's paradox loses its stakes. 'hardest hitters' loses its prize-fight frame. The Bull Run and Trent reactions lose their stated reasons, and Sumner's role in the father's isolation becomes implicit.

Locations and actors are clear: Maurigy's, Mansfield Street, Fryston, Mount Felix and the Lodge. The three secretaries and the Minister's absence are kept, and paragraph 5 now correctly names 'the Government'. The only soft spot is 'no one cared to hurry it', which is slightly vague now that 'Europe' is gone (folded into F6).
The chapter has little speech. 'amhandheggsir', 'Quel chien de pays!', 'Surtout point de zele!' and the Gladstone quotation are all kept with correct attribution.

The 'probably intended' hedge and the 'did not then know' boundary survive. Two of the young man's counterweights are cut: his suspicion of American sources for the prejudice, and his admission that he met no rudeness that year.

No premature disclosure. The 'nearly seven years longer' line stays a forward glance, and the Legation's beliefs about Russell stay 1861 perceptions. Losing the opening 'white beard' retrospect slightly mutes the old narrator, but later cues ('next thirty years', 'several generations') keep the distance.

The signature lines survive. Some aphoristic closers and build-ups are lost: the 'thought it worse' reversal, the cabin-boy counterfactual, 'Any winter in London... first winter is the most trying', and Milnes's 'good-nature of London'.

The ledger of failed education, the absurd son versus the lucky father, and 'He meant to go home' all hold. Cutting 'began to doubt whether secretaries were meant to be useful' weakens a seed for the 'useful' theme, but paragraph 19 still carries that theme.
All four dependencies are intact at both endpoints in this run's partner revisions (011, 012, 013, 017).

findings.claim: The revision cuts three things the first draft kept: the realization that the shock was likely fatal to his father, the expectation of going home within weeks, and the later chill at what would have happened had the father proved unfit as Sumner thought. Without them, the claim that the son's confidence proved him unfit has little ground.
findings.counterevidence: The next sentence ('It never entered his mind that his father might lose his nerve') partly supplies the missing contrast.

evidence.quote: Yet he realized that to his father it was likely to be fatal. The chances were great that the whole family would turn round and go home within a few weeks.
he grew cold at the idea of his situation had his father then shown himself what Sumner thought him to be--unfit for his post
That the private secretary was unfit for his post--trifling though it were--was proved by his unreflecting confidence in his father.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore 'Yet he realized that to his father it was likely to be fatal.' and the clause 'had his father then shown himself what Sumner thought him to be--unfit for his post'.
findings.plan_relation: Required: the plan lists 'Henry's dullness of comprehension; his unreflecting confidence in his father' as essential.
findings.reader_effect: The irony depends on the father's possible failure being a live danger the son never weighed. The paradox now reads as a bare assertion, and the recognition shock loses its immediate consequence.
findings.title: Paragraph 9 'unfit' paradox loses its stakes and its counterfactual

strengths: All eight verbatim passages (V1–V8) survive intact in context, including the leap-frog payoff and 'He was mistaken--of course!'.
The Trent sequence keeps the three cheering secretaries, the telegram to Fryston, the Prince Consort's death and the 'nearly seven years' forward glance.
The Mill anecdote keeps the Lodge setting and Henry's insistence that Mill's assent, not the claret, was to blame.
Paragraph 5 replaces the first draft's ambiguous 'they' with 'the Government', clarifying who sent Cassius Clay.
Russell is consistently 'Lord John Russell', avoiding the source's anachronistic 'Earl Russell' in this chapter.
summary: The revision is faithful in its main lines. It keeps every verbatim passage, all continuity checks and all four dependencies. It fixes the first draft's loose 'they' in the Clay passage. Most of its new cuts are defensible, but several remove setup or turning phrases the surviving text still leans on: the stakes behind the 'unfit' paradox, the closing reversal of the Maurigy's joke, the prize-fight frame that 'hardest hitters' assumes, and the reasons behind the Bull Run resignation and the Trent cheers. None of these is a blocker; all are small editorial repairs or tradeoffs.
